newsitem.title: BOSNIA: NATO troops search tense Bosnian hamlet for arms.
newsitem.headline: NATO troops search tense Bosnian hamlet for arms.

text.p: NATO peacekeeping troops raided a tense Bosnian boundary village on Thursday in search of weapons and other contraband but found none, the U.S. army said.

The "aggressive search-and-seizure operation" was mounted in Jusici, a hamlet on the edge of Serb-controlled territory in northeast Bosnia now resettled by Moslem refugees under terms of the 1995 Dayton peace treaty.

The influx has led to bombings of empty homes in several hamlets being repopulated by Moslems, some of whom brought in weapons secretly in violation of NATO's demilitarisation regime in Bosnia, Western sources say.
NATO wants to prevent returning Moslems from smuggling in arms and provoking attacks by Serbs.

"IFOR (NATO peace Implementation Force) soldiers attempted to uncover arms and munitions that were suspected to be hidden in the homes of (Jusici)," said a statement from U.S. army division headquarters in Tuzla sent to news agencies.
"The village and the surrounding area have experienced unrest in the past six weeks with homes of would-be resettlers destroyed by fire and explosions," it said.
"The operation was a complete success, with 109 homes and buildings searched and no weapons or other contraband found."

Soldiers from eight nations in IFOR took part in the raid, part of a wider effort to enforce a ban on weapons in the Zone of Separation demarcating Bosnia's Serb and Moslem-Croat entities, the statement said.

Moslem, Serb and Croat refugees from the 1992-95 war have announced plans to form a coalition to resist attempts by local nationalist authorities to discourage the return of displaced people, in part by terror bombings.
More than 90 Moslem houses and two mosques were destroyed in several abandoned villages near Serb-held Prijedor in northwest Bosnia on one day last week.
In Croat-held Drvar to the south, 65 Serb houses in two villages were blown up over a period of several days.

The U.S.-brokered Dayton treaty guaranteed refugees the right to reclaim homes. But separatist authorities across Bosnia have frustrated repatriation schemes in most areas and moved their own refugees into abandoned homes.
